claim: Cannabis is the most consumed illicit psychoactive drug in the world.
source: Cannabis, the most consumed illicit psychoactive drug in the world, is increasingly used by pregnant women.
evidence: Supported by citation to U.N Office on Drugs and Crime, 2022 in the Introduction section.

claim: Cannabinoid receptors are expressed in the early embryo.
source: However, while cannabinoid receptors are expressed in the early embryo, the impact of phytocannabinoids exposure on early embryonic processes is lacking.
evidence: Supported by citation to Paria et al., 1995 in the Introduction section.

claim: Δ9-THC increases the proliferation of naive mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs).
source: We demonstrate that Δ9-THC increases the proliferation of naive mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) but not of their primed counterpart.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased viable cell numbers and BrdU incorporation in ESCs exposed to Δ9-THC (Figure 1C and 1D).

claim: Δ9-THC does not increase the proliferation of primed pluripotent stem cells (EpiLCs).
source: We demonstrate that Δ9-THC increases the proliferation of naive mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) but not of their primed counterpart.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant increase in viable cell numbers or BrdU incorporation in EpiLCs (Figure 1F and 1G).

claim: The increased proliferation of ESCs by Δ9-THC is dependent on CB1 receptor binding.
source: Surprisingly, this increased proliferation, dependent on the CB1 receptor binding, is only associated with moderate transcriptomic changes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that CB1 antagonist SR141716 abolished Δ9-THC-induced ESC proliferation (Figure 2D).

claim: Δ9-THC exposure in ESCs is associated with moderate transcriptomic changes.
source: Surprisingly, this increased proliferation, dependent on the CB1 receptor binding, is only associated with moderate transcriptomic changes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing low numbers of differentially expressed genes in ESCs (Figure 5C).

claim: Δ9-THC increases glycolytic rates in ESCs.
source: Instead, Δ9-THC capitalizes on ESCs' metabolic bivalence by increasing their glycolytic rates and anabolic capabilities.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse bioanalyzer measurements showing increased extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in ESCs exposed to Δ9-THC (Figure 3D).

claim: Δ9-THC increases anabolic capabilities in ESCs.
source: Instead, Δ9-THC capitalizes on ESCs' metabolic bivalence by increasing their glycolytic rates and anabolic capabilities.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data showing upregulation of metabolic pathways involved in synthesis of amino acids, nucleotides, and fatty acids (Figure 4D).

claim: A memory of metabolic rewiring by Δ9-THC is retained throughout differentiation to Primordial Germ Cell-Like Cells (PGCLCs) in the absence of direct exposure.
source: A memory of this metabolic rewiring is retained throughout differentiation to Primordial Germ Cell-Like Cells in the absence of direct exposure and is associated with an alteration of their transcriptional profile.
evidence: Supported by metabolic profiling showing increased NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios and mitochondrial activity in PGCLCs derived from Δ9-THC-exposed ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 7B and 7C).

claim: Metabolic memory of Δ9-THC exposure in PGCLCs is associated with an alteration of their transcriptional profile.
source: A memory of this metabolic rewiring is retained throughout differentiation to Primordial Germ Cell-Like Cells in the absence of direct exposure and is associated with an alteration of their transcriptional profile.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing significant transcriptional changes in PGCLCs derived from Δ9-THC-exposed precursors (Figure 7E).

claim: In the United States, an estimated 49.6 million people consumed cannabis at least once in 2020.
source: In the United States, an estimated 49.6 million people, roughly 18% of the population, consumed cannabis at least once in 2020, with indications that these numbers will likely increase in the coming years as attitudes and regulations change (Mennis et al., 2023; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mennis et al., 2023 and Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2020.

claim: Between 7% and 12% of expecting women report cannabis use, predominantly during the first trimester.
source: In particular, between 7% and 12% of expecting women report cannabis use, predominantly during the first trimester, to alleviate the symptoms of morning sickness (Chabarria et al., 2016; Volkow et al., 2019; Young-Wolff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chabarria et al., 2016; Volkow et al., 2019; Young-Wolff et al., 2018.

claim: Δ9-THC is chiefly responsible for the psychoactivity of cannabis.
source: Among the several hundred unique phytocannabinoids present in Cannabis sativa, (−)-trans-Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (Δ9-THC) is chiefly responsible for the psychoactivity of cannabis (Andre et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andre et al., 2016.

claim: The level of Δ9-THC in recreational cannabis now commonly accounts for 20% of total compounds.
source: As a result, the level of Δ9-THC in recreational cannabis has increased over the last 10 years and now commonly accounts for 20% of total compounds (Chandra et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chandra et al., 2019.

claim: The psychoactive effects of Δ9-THC arise from its binding and activation of the CB1 receptor.
source: The psychoactive effects of Δ9-THC arise from its binding and subsequent activation of the G-protein-coupled cannabinoid receptor CB1 largely expressed in the central nervous system (Pacher et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pacher et al., 2020.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure durably alters metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic programs in the brain.
source: In this context, Δ9-THC exposure has been shown to durably alter metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic programs in the brain (Bénard et al., 2012; Prini et al., 2018; Szutorisz and Hurd, 2018; Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bénard et al., 2012; Prini et al., 2018; Szutorisz and Hurd, 2018; Watson et al., 2015.

claim: CB1 is expressed in the male and female reproductive tracts, in the pre-implantation embryo, and in the placenta.
source: Data shows CB1 expression in the male and the female reproductive tracts, in the pre-implantation embryo and in the placenta (Lo et al., 2022; Paria et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lo et al., 2022; Paria et al., 1995.

claim: Exposure to cannabis is associated with reduced fertility, decreased testis weight and sperm count, and impairment of embryo implantation.
source: In animal models as well as in humans, exposure to cannabis is associated with reduced fertility, decreased testis weight and sperm count, and impairment of embryo implantation (Lo et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lo et al., 2022.

claim: Cannabis exposure in males is correlated with an alteration of the sperm transcriptome and epigenome.
source: In males, these effects are correlated with an alteration of the sperm transcriptome and epigenome (Murphy et al., 2018; Osborne et al., 2020; Schrott and Murphy, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2018; Osborne et al., 2020; Schrott and Murphy, 2020.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure is associated with long-lasting adverse effects, with exposures in parents affecting the offspring.
source: Epidemiological evidence also indicates that Δ9-THC exposure is associated with long-lasting adverse effects, with exposures in parents affecting the offspring (Smith et al., 2020; Szutorisz and Hurd, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2020; Szutorisz and Hurd, 2018.

claim: Progression through states of pluripotency is controlled by metabolic reprogramming in the early mammalian embryo.
source: Progression through states of pluripotency is controlled by metabolic reprogramming in the early mammalian embryo (Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are naïve PSCs that are functionally equivalent to the inner cell mass (ICM) of the E3.5 preimplantation mouse blastocyst.
source: For instance, mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) are naïve PSCs that are functionally equivalent to the inner cell mass (ICM) of the E3.5 preimplantation mouse blastocyst (Nichols and Smith, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols and Smith, 2009.

claim: The extended developmental potential of mouse ESCs is associated with their metabolic bivalence.
source: The extended developmental potential of mouse ESCs is associated with their metabolic bivalence, as these cells rely on both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation for energy production.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about ESC metabolism.

claim: Differentiation of naïve ESCs into primed PSCs such as epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs) is accompanied by a metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis.
source: Differentiation of naïve ESCs into primed PSCs such as epiblast-like cells (EpiLCs) is accompanied by an important metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis, in link with a highly proliferative phenotype and a more restricted developmental potential (Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021; Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Primordial germ cells (PGCs) are the embryonic precursors of gametes in metazoans.
source: Primordial germ cells (PGCs), the embryonic precursors of gametes in metazoans (Hayashi et al., 2007; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018), are considered dormant totipotent cells because they possess the unique ability to reacquire totipotency upon fertilization (Hayashi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2007; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018.

claim: PGCs possess the unique ability to reacquire totipotency upon fertilization.
source: Primordial germ cells (PGCs), the embryonic precursors of gametes in metazoans (Hayashi et al., 2007; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018), are considered dormant totipotent cells because they possess the unique ability to reacquire totipotency upon fertilization (Hayashi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hayashi et al., 2017.

claim: In the mouse embryo, the precursors to PGCs arise around embryonic day 6.25 (E6.25) from formative pluripotent cells in the epiblast.
source: In the mouse embryo, the precursors to PGCs arise around embryonic day 6.25 (E6.25) from formative pluripotent cells in the epiblast (Kinoshita et al., 2021; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kinoshita et al., 2021; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2018.

claim: Progressive increase in oxidative phosphorylation correlates with the specification and differentiation from epiblast PSCs towards PGCs.
source: Progressive increase in oxidative phosphorylation correlates with the specification and differentiation from epiblast PSCs towards PGCs, a process that can be replicated in vitro by inducing PGC-like cells (PGCLCs) from EpiLCs (Hayashi et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2022.

claim: The extensive metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic reprogramming that PGCs undergo during their development has been proposed to be uniquely sensitive to environmental insults.
source: In particular, the extensive metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic reprogramming that PGCs undergo during their development has been proposed to be uniquely sensitive to environmental insults, with potential consequences in the offspring (Verdikt et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verdikt et al., 2022.

claim: The viability of ESCs exposed to Δ9-THC was not significantly altered until the maximal dose of 100 µM.
source: The viability of ESCs exposed to increasing concentrations of Δ9-THC for 48 hr was not significantly altered until the maximal dose of 100 µM, subsequently serving as a positive control, at which only 13.17% of cells remained alive (Figure 1B, p=5.10–15, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of viable ESCs significantly increased at doses between 10 nM and 1 µM of Δ9-THC.
source: While no significant changes in viability were observed between 10 nM and 1 µM Δ9-THC, the number of viable ESCs significantly increased by 1.69, 1.52 and 1.28-fold, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 1C, p=0.002, p=0.01 and p=0.03 for 10 nM, 100 nM and 1 µM of Δ9-THC, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The number of viable ESCs significantly increased at doses of Δ9-THC as low as 1 nM.
source: Of note, the number of viable ESCs significantly increased for doses of Δ9-THC as low as 1 nM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and, 0.59-fold increase, p=0.0005, unpaired T-test), corresponding to doses found in users of 'light cannabis' products (Pacifici et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Pacifici et al., 2020.

claim: The percentage of BrdU-positive ESCs significantly increased between 10 nM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC.
source: The percentage of BrdU-positive ESCs significantly increased between 10 nM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 1D, p=0.01, p=0.001, p=0.05 and p=0.01 for 10 nM, 100 nM, 1 µM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, a significantly higher proportion of ESCs were in the G2/M phase.
source: Co-staining with DAPI (4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) to analyze the cell cycle showed that, at 100 nM of Δ9-THC, a significantly higher proportion of cells were in the G2/M phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and, 0.76-fold increase, p=0.02, unpaired T-test), consistent with cellular proliferation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The proliferative effect of Δ9-THC exposure on ESCs is sex-independent.
source: Finally, whereas the present data was obtained using female ESCs, the proliferative effect of Δ9-THC exposure on ESCs was also observed in male ESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that proliferation is sex-independent.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly alter cellular viability until the dose of 100 µM.
source: Akin to ESCs, Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly alter cellular viability until the dose of 100 µM (Figure 1E, 11.56% of viable cells, p=1.6–13, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly increase the number of viable cells or the percentage of BrdU-positive cells.
source: However, contrary to ESCs, Δ9-THC exposure in EpiLCs did not significantly increase the number of viable cells nor the percentage of BrdU-positive cells (Figure 1F and Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claim: At 10 µM of Δ9-THC, viable EpiLCs numbers and BrdU-positive EpiLCs decreased compared to the mock-treated condition.
source: For the dose of 10 µM of Δ9-THC, viable EpiLCs numbers and BrdU-positive EpiLCs decreased compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 1F, 1.53-fold decrease, p=0.0007, Figure 1G, 1.42-fold decrease, p=0.0024, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claim: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) resemble a primed pluripotent state, akin to mouse EpiLCs.
source: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) differ from their murine counterparts, particularly because they resemble a primed pluripotent state, akin to mouse EpiLCs (Weinberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberger et al., 2016.

claim: Cell viability of hESCs continuously exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC was not significantly impacted.
source: Cell viability of hESCS continuously exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC was not significantly impacted (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: hESCs number was significantly decreased upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: However, hESCs number was significantly decreased upon Δ9-THC exposure (Figure 1—figure supplements 4B and 1.26-fold decrease, p=0.004, unpaired T-test), in a similar trend as observed with mouse EpiLCs (Figure 1E and Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: CB1 was expressed at the same levels at the cell surface of both ESCs and EpiLCs.
source: Western-blot analysis of membrane proteins revealed however that CB1 was expressed at the same levels at the cell surface of both ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Rimonabant pre-treatment abolished Δ9-THC-induced ESCs increased cell number at 100 nM Δ9-THC.
source: Rimonabant pre-treatment did not significantly alter the viability of ESCs compared to conditions exposed to Δ9-THC only (Figure 2C) but abolished Δ9-THC-induced ESCs increased cell number at 100 nM Δ9-THC (Figure 2D, 1.53-fold decrease, p=1.66–05, when comparing 100 nM of Δ9-THC+/-1 µM of SR141716, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SR141716 pre-treatment reduced ESC cell number compared to control, suggesting a basal role for CB1 in promoting proliferation.
source: Notably, SR141716 pre-treatment, while not altering cell viability, reduced cell number compared to control, suggesting a basal role for CB1 in promoting proliferation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and inference from the observed reduction in cell number.

claim: The ratio of NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H significantly increased in ESCs at doses between 10 nM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC.
source: In ESCs, the ratio of NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H significantly increased 1.57, 1.54, 1.29, and 1.38 -fold, for 10 nM, 100 nM, 1 µM, and 10 µM of Δ9-THC, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 3B, p=2.87–06, p=8.01–05, p=0.03, and p=0.0003 for 10 nM, 100 nM, 1 µM and 10 µM of Δ9-THC, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No significant increase was observed in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios in exposed EpiLCs.
source: In contrast, no significant increase was observed in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios in exposed EpiLCs (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios significantly decreased at 10 µM of Δ9-THC in EpiLCs.
source: Consistent with the impact of continuous Δ9-THC exposure on EpiLCs viability (Figure 1H), the NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios significantly decreased at 10 µM of Δ9-THC in EpiLCs (Figure 3B, 59% decrease for 10 µM of Δ9-THC compared to the mock-treated condition, p=6.55–09, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios were slightly but significantly decreased at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in hESCs.
source: Of note, the NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratios were slightly but significantly decreased at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in hESCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, 0.09-fold decrease, p=0.04, unpaired T-test), in agreement with the deleterious effect of Δ9-THC on cell number (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant increase in mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) associated with the mitochondrial stain was observed at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in ESCs.
source: A significant increase in mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) associated with the mitochondrial stain was observed at 100 nM of Δ9-THC in ESCs (Figure 3C, p=0.02, unpaired T-test), indicating that, at this dose, the observed increase in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H could be explained by higher mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No change in EpiLCs' mitochondrial activity was detected upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: By contrast, no change in EpiLCs' mitochondrial activity was detected (Figure 3C), consistent with these cells relying on glycolysis for energy production (Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and citations to Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021.

claim: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal glycolytic capacity of both ESCs and EpiLCs increased significantly.
source: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal glycolytic capacity of both ESCs and EpiLCs increased significantly (Figure 3D, 15% increase, p=0.03 and 22% increase, p=0.03 for ESCs and EpiLCs, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A significant decrease in glycolytic capacity was observed at 10 µM of Δ9-THC in both ESCs and EpiLCs.
source: In both cell types, a significant decrease in glycolytic capacity was observed at 10 µM of Δ9-THC (Figure 3D, 39.8% reduction, p=0.0006 and 44.8% reduction, p=0.0001, for ESCs and EpiLCs, respectively, compared to the mock-treated condition, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The maximal glycolytic capacity of EpiLCs in the untreated condition was higher than that of ESCs.
source: Of note, the maximal glycolytic capacity of EpiLCs in the untreated condition was higher than the one of ESCs, in agreement with their metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis (Figure 3D, 7.88% higher ECAR rate in mock-treated EpiLCs compared to mock-treated ESCs, p=0.03, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs was significantly increased compared to the mock-treated condition.
source: In addition, at 100 nM of Δ9-THC, the maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs was significantly increased compared to the mock-treated condition (Figure 3E, 21.8% increase, p=0.03, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The increase in maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs at 100 nM Δ9-THC was observed only for maximal capacity, not for basal or ATP-linked respiration.
source: This increase was observed only for the maximal respiratory capacity of ESCs, but not for basal respiration, nor for ATP-linked respiration (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that Δ9-THC impact on mitochondrial respiration does not support increased energetic production.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Increasing doses of Δ9-THC did not alter the maximal respiratory capacity of EpiLCs.
source: In agreement with EpiLCs' metabolic shift towards a glycolytic phenotype, increasing doses of Δ9-THC did not alter their maximal respiratory capacity (Figure 3E), nor their global oxygen consumption rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Of the 126 metabolites detected in ESCs, 39 were significantly upregulated upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Of the 126 metabolites detected in ESCs, 39 were significantly upregulated (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and only two metabolites – NAPDH and Adenine – were significantly downregulated.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Of the 138 metabolites detected in EpiLCs, 95 were significantly upregulated upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Of the 138 metabolites detected in EpiLCs, 95 were significantly upregulated (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and only one metabolite – NAPDH – was significantly downregulated.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pyruvate metabolism and glycolysis were upregulated in both ESCs and EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Indeed, amongst the 25 metabolic pathways upregulated, pyruvate metabolism and glycolysis were detected in both ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 4D and Figure 4E, respectively).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics pathway analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4E.

claim: Increased mitochondrial respiration was seen in ESCs with the enrichment of (ubi)quinone metabolism.
source: Increased mitochondrial respiration was also seen in ESCs with the enrichment of (ubi)quinone metabolism, indicating an increased synthesis of ubiquinone that serves as an electron carrier in oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics pathway analysis and inference about ubiquinone function.

claim: The ratio of glutathione in its reduced to oxidized form (GSH/GSSG) was unchanged in both stem cell types in response to Δ9-THC.
source: Of note, metabolite measurements showed that the ratio of glutathione in its reduced to oxidated form (GSH/GSSG) was unchanged in both stem cell types in response to Δ9-THC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the increased mitochondrial respiration does not cause an overt elevation of oxidative stress.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure elicited an increase in metabolic pathways that feed anabolic reactions in both ESCs and EpiLCs.
source: Importantly, and in agreement with the PCA, in both ESCs and EpiLCs, Δ9-THC exposure elicited an increase in metabolic pathways that feed anabolic reactions, in particular contributing to the synthesis of amino acids (tyrosine, tryptophan, arginine, alanine, valine, (iso)leucine, etc.), nucleotides ('Pyrimidine metabolism', 'Purine metabolism'), NAD(P)+ ('Nicotinate and nicotinamide metabolism') and fatty acids ('Butanoate metabolism'; Figure 4D and Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics pathway analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4E.

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis by 2-DG abrogated the Δ9-THC-induced increase in both ESC cell number and NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H levels.
source: Importantly, glycolytic inhibition by 2-DG abrogated the Δ9-THC-induced increase in both cell number and NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H levels (Figure 4G and Figure 4H, 1.39-fold reduction and p=5.56–05 and 1.68-fold reduction and p=0.0064, respectively, when comparing 100 nM of Δ9-THC+/-10 mM 2-DG, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4H.

claim: Exposure to Δ9-THC increases anabolism in both ESCs and EpiLCs, but this increased anabolism only supports cellular proliferation in ESCs.
source: Thus, exposure to Δ9-THC increases anabolism in both ESCs and EpiLCs, however, this increased anabolism only supports cellular proliferation in ESCs.
evidence: Supported by integration of metabolomics and proliferation data.

claim: The vast majority of data variation in transcriptome analysis could be attributed to the cell type rather than to Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Unsupervised exploration of the global transcriptome by PCA revealed that the vast majority of data variation could be attributed to the cell type (PC1, accounting for 98% of the variation) rather than to Δ9-THC exposure (PC2, accounting for 1% of the variation, Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure does not appear to influence the differentiation dynamics from ESCs to EpiLCs.
source: In addition, mining for the expression of pluripotency markers after Δ9-THC exposure suggested that Δ9-THC does not appear to influence the differentiation dynamics from ESCs to EpiLCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure only moderately impacts ESC and EpiLC transcriptomes.
source: We identified a low number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in both ESCs and EpiLCs (Figure 5C and Figure 5D, respectively), indicating that Δ9-THC exposure only moderately impacts ESC and EpiLC transcriptomes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5D.

claim: In ESCs, only 12 genes were significantly upregulated with a log2(fold-change) >0.5 and only 9 were significantly downregulated at the same threshold upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: In ESCs, only 12 genes were significantly upregulated with a log2(fold-change) >0.5 and only 9 were significantly downregulated at the same threshold (Figure 5C, significance corresponds to adjusted P-value ≤0.05).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GO terms associated with metabolic pathways involved in anabolism were significantly over-represented for upregulated genes in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
source: In particular, GO terms associated with metabolic pathways involved in anabolism were significantly over-represented for upregulated genes in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure (Figure 5E), such as: 'Cellular aromatic compound metabolic process', 'Cellular nitrogen compound biosynthetic process', 'Organonitrogen compound metabolic process'.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: GO terms associated with metabolism were not found within the upregulated DEGs in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: In contrast, GO terms associated with metabolism were not found within the upregulated DEGs in EpiLCs.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis results.

claim: Several GO terms relating to alterations in cellular components were enriched in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: However, several GO terms relating to alterations in cellular components were enriched in EpiLCs (Figure 5E), such as: 'Organelle organization', 'Cellular component organization or biogenesis', 'Microtubule-based process'.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The expression levels of multiple epigenetic modifiers were significantly altered in either ESCs or EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Data shows that the expression levels of multiple epigenetic modifiers were significantly altered, albeit at a low level, in either ESCs or EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure (|log2(fold-change)|>0.25, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression levels of the DNA dioxygenase Tet2 were significantly increased in EpiLCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
source: In particular, the expression levels of the DNA dioxygenase Tet2 were significantly increased in EpiLCs following Δ9-THC exposure, which would contribute to changes in DNA methylation dynamics and differentiation potential (Sohni et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and citation to Sohni et al., 2015.

claim: The expression of the histone deacetylases Hdac5 and Hdac11 were significantly decreased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
source: The expression of the two histone deacetylases Hdac5 and Hdac11 were significantly decreased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure, while the expression of the histone phosphorylase Rps6ka5 increased under the same conditions.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of the histone phosphorylase Rps6ka5 increased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure.
source: The expression of the two histone deacetylases Hdac5 and Hdac11 were significantly decreased in ESCs following Δ9-THC exposure, while the expression of the histone phosphorylase Rps6ka5 increased under the same conditions.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of the histone methyltransferase Kmt2c was significantly increased in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: In EpiLCs, the expression of the histone methyltransferase Kmt2c and of the regulators of histone ubiquitination Dzip3 and Mysm1 were all significantly increased upon Δ9-THC exposure.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of the regulators of histone ubiquitination Dzip3 and Mysm1 were significantly increased in EpiLCs upon Δ9-THC exposure.
source: In EpiLCs, the expression of the histone methyltransferase Kmt2c and of the regulators of histone ubiquitination Dzip3 and Mysm1 were all significantly increased upon Δ9-THC exposure.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: RNA-seq data suggests the existence of an epigenetic remodelling following Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Collectively, RNA-seq data suggests the existence of an epigenetic remodelling following Δ9-THC exposure, although further analysis of the respective epigenetic marks associated with these modifiers is needed.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing altered expression of epigenetic modifiers.

claim: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, there was a significant decrease in double-negative (DN) cells and a corresponding significant increase in single-positive (SP) and double-positive (DP) PGCLCs.
source: Specifically, at 100 nM Δ9-THC, a significant decrease in DN was observed, with a corresponding significant increase of 1.14-fold in SP and of 1.64-fold in DP cells (Figure 6C, p=0.0002, p=0.05, and p=1.55–06 for 100 nM of Δ9-THC in DN, SP, and DP populations respectively compared to the mock-treated condition, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The same pattern of increased PGCLC induction was observed when male ESCs and EpiLCs exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC were differentiated into PGCLCs.
source: The same pattern was observed when male ESCs and EpiLCs exposed to 100 nM of Δ9-THC were differentiated in PGCLCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, a smaller proportion of DN cells underwent two or three mitotic divisions compared to the control.
source: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, a smaller proportion of DN cells underwent two or three mitotic divisions compared to the control (Figure 6D, 1.14-fold fewer cells and 1.12-fold fewer cells, p=0.05 and p=0.04 for 2 divisions and 3 divisions, respectively, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by proliferation tracing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: At 100 nM Δ9-THC, a significantly higher proportion of SP and DP cells underwent three mitotic divisions compared to the control.
source: In parallel, for the same dose, a significantly higher proportion of SP and DP cells underwent three mitotic divisions compared to the control (Figure 6D, 1.24-fold and 1.11-fold, p=0.03 and p=0.0035, for 3 divisions in SP and DP cells, compared to the control, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by proliferation tracing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The higher number of PGCLCs observed upon Δ9-THC exposure originates from their increased proliferation during their specification and differentiation.
source: These results, therefore, indicate that the higher number of PGCLCs observed upon Δ9-THC exposure originates from their increased proliferation during their specification and differentiation.
evidence: Supported by proliferation tracing data and inference.

claim: No ∆9-THC could be detected in day 5 embryoid bodies, indicating that ∆9-THC does not persist to levels higher than the limit of detection of mass spectrometry (1 ng/mL).
source: Data shows that no ∆9-THC could be detected in day 5 embryoid bodies, indicating that ∆9-THC does not persist to levels higher than the limit of detection of mass spectrometry (1 ng/mL).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The proliferative effects in PGCLCs are not due to residual ∆9-THC persisting in the cells during differentiation.
source: This suggests that the proliferative effects are not due to residual ∆9-THC persisting in the cells during differentiation towards PGCLCs.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data showing no detectable ∆9-THC in day 5 embryoid bodies.

claim: Δ9-THC causes an alteration of the developmental kinetics that PGCLCs normally undergo, even in the absence of direct continuous exposure.
source: Thus, Δ9-THC causes an alteration of the developmental kinetics that PGCLCs normally undergo, even in the absence of direct continuous exposure.
evidence: Supported by proliferation and induction efficiency data in PGCLCs derived from exposed precursors.

claim: NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratio in whole day 5 embryoid bodies deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs increased 1.17-fold compared to those deriving from mock-treated cells.
source: First, NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H assessment revealed a modest but significant 1.17-fold increase in NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H ratio in whole day 5 embryoid bodies deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs compared to those deriving from mock-treated cells (Figure 7B, P=0.01, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A significant increase in mitochondrial membrane potential (MFI) was observed in DN, SP and DP populations deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs compared to those deriving from mock controls.
source: A significant increase in MFI was observed in DN, SP and DP populations deriving from exposed ESCs +EpiLCs compared to those deriving from mock controls (Figure 7C, 1.17, 1.16, 1.23 -fold, p=0.006, p=0.05 and p=0.01 for DN, SP, and DP, respectively, unpaired T-test).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The metabolic changes induced by Δ9-THC prior to PGCLCs induction and differentiation are not reset during the profound reprogramming that PGCLCs undergo.
source: These results indicate that the metabolic changes induced by Δ9-THC prior to PGCLCs induction and differentiation are not reset during the profound reprogramming that PGCLCs undergo.
evidence: Supported by metabolic profiling data showing sustained changes in PGCLCs.

claim: PCA of DP PGCLCs transcriptome delineated a transcriptional signature of prior Δ9-THC exposure.
source: Unsupervised analysis of the global transcriptome in DP PGCLCs by PCA delineated a transcriptional signature of prior Δ9-THC exposure (Figure 7D, PC1 accounting for 59% of the variance and PC2 accounting for 24% of variance).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Most of the significant transcriptional change in DP PGCLCs was towards downregulation rather than upregulation.
source: Volcano plot of DEGs between DP PGCLCs deriving from mock- or 100 nM Δ9-THC-exposed ESCs and EpiLCs revealed that most of the significant transcriptional change was towards downregulation rather than upregulation (Figure 7E, 11 genes were significantly upregulated whereas 97 were significantly downregulated, |log2(fold-change)|>0.25 and adjusted p-value ≤0.05).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: All GO terms enriched for upregulated DEGs in PGCLCs corresponded to metabolic processes involved in oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Despite the low number of upregulated DEGs, the functional annotation of their associated GO terms showed that all terms enriched corresponded to metabolic processes involved in oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 7F, 'Aerobic electron transport chain', 'Mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I assembly', 'Electron transport couple proton transport').
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The metabolic changes induced by exposure to Δ9-THC prior to PGCLCs specification are retained through transcriptional reprogramming.
source: Thus, our data indicate that the metabolic changes induced by exposure to Δ9-THC prior to PGCLCs specification are retained through transcriptional reprogramming.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis showing upregulation of oxidative phosphorylation genes.

claim: Pre-specification Δ9-THC exposure increases PGCLCs number and mitochondrial activity.
source: Importantly, while our results show that pre-specification Δ9-THC exposure increases PGCLCs number and mitochondrial activity, the functional annotation of GO terms associated with downregulated DEGs suggests degradation of PGCLCs quality.
evidence: Supported by proliferation data and metabolic profiling.

claim: The functional annotation of GO terms associated with downregulated DEGs in PGCLCs suggests degradation of PGCLCs quality.
source: Importantly, while our results show that pre-specification Δ9-THC exposure increases PGCLCs number and mitochondrial activity, the functional annotation of GO terms associated with downregulated DEGs suggests degradation of PGCLCs quality.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis showing downregulation of genes related to cellular structure and adhesion.

claim: Several GO terms relating to alterations in structural cellular components were enriched in downregulated genes in PGCLCs.
source: Indeed, and reminiscent of GO terms observed in EpiLCs, several GO terms relating to alterations in structural cellular components ('Anatomical structure morphogenesis', 'Cellular anatomical entity'), and in particular the interface with the extracellular environment ('External encapsulating structure organization', 'Membrane', 'Cell periphery', 'Extracellular region', 'Extracellular space', 'Extracellular matrix structural constituent') were enriched (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: GO terms associated with cell adhesion and junction were enriched in downregulated genes in PGCLCs.
source: Furthermore, GO terms associated with cell adhesion and junction ('Cell adhesion', 'Cell migration', 'Collagen metabolic process', 'Cell junction', 'Anchoring junction', 'Collagen trimer') were also enriched in downregulated genes.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure in ESCs and EpiLCs durably alters their metabolome and these changes are carried through PGCLCs specification and differentiation, leading to an alteration of PGCLCs transcriptional program.
source: Together, our data show that Δ9-THC exposure in ESCs and EpiLCs durably alters their metabolome and that these changes are carried through PGCLCs specification and differentiation, leading to an alteration of PGCLCs transcriptional program (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by integration of metabolomics and transcriptomics data across developmental stages.

claim: Cannabis use directly alters adult male fertility and causes abnormal embryo implantation.
source: Cannabis use directly alters adult male fertility and causes abnormal embryo implantation (Lo et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lo et al., 2022.

claim: This study is the first to shed light on the impact of Δ9-THC at early embryonic developmental stages.
source: Using a well-characterized in vitro model of early embryonic differentiation events culminating in the differentiation of PGCLCs, our study is the first to shed light on the impact of Δ9-THC at these stages which unfold during the first trimester in humans (Chabarria et al., 2016; Volkow et al., 2019; Young-Wolff et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by the novelty of the experimental approach and citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Differential expression and use of cannabinoid receptors on the surface of exposed cells have been shown to correlate with Δ9-THC proliferative phenotypes.
source: Differential expression and use of cannabinoid receptors on the surface of exposed cells have been shown to correlate with Δ9-THC proliferative phenotypes (Galve-Roperh et al., 2013; Preet et al., 2008; Takeda et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galve-Roperh et al., 2013; Preet et al., 2008; Takeda et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2016.

claim: Δ9-THC is a known perturbator of mitochondrial function in the central nervous system.
source: Because Δ9-THC is a known perturbator of mitochondrial function as previously described in the central nervous system (Bartova and Birmingham, 1976; Bénard et al., 2012), we studied the metabolic impact of its exposure in ESCs and EpiLCs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartova and Birmingham, 1976; Bénard et al., 2012.

claim: The metabolic signatures associated with Δ9-THC exposure are reminiscent of those inherently occurring during naïve-to-prime transition.
source: Thus, the metabolic signatures associated with Δ9-THC exposure are reminiscent of those inherently occurring during naïve-to-prime transition, during which increased aerobic glycolytic rates feed anabolic reactions ultimately fueling proliferation (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011).
evidence: Supported by comparison with established knowledge and citation to Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011.

claim: Δ9-THC exposure elicits a reprogramming of ESCs that coaxes them to rely more on aerobic glycolysis, drives anabolic pathways, and leads to their proliferation.
source: Together, we propose that Δ9-THC exposure elicits a reprogramming of ESCs that (1) coaxes them to rely more on aerobic glycolysis, (2) drives anabolic pathways, and therefore (3) leads to their proliferation.
evidence: Supported by integration of metabolomics, bioenergetics, and proliferation data.

claim: In EpiLCs, the impact of Δ9-THC exposure is not sufficient to override the cellular and metabolic programs of these already highly proliferative cells that are fully reliant on aerobic glycolysis.
source: In EpiLCs, the impact of Δ9-THC exposure is not sufficient to override the cellular and metabolic programs of these already highly proliferative cells that are fully reliant on aerobic glycolysis (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by comparison of metabolic and proliferation data between ESCs and EpiLCs.

claim: During PGCLCs differentiation, metabolic reprogramming and increased oxidative phosphorylation play a critical role in the reacquisition of an extended developmental potential.
source: In particular, during PGCLCs differentiation, metabolic reprogramming and increased oxidative phosphorylation play a critical role in the reacquisition of an extended developmental potential (Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2017; Verdikt and Allard, 2021.

claim: In the absence of direct or indirect continuous exposure, Δ9-THC still has lasting consequences on the metabolome of embryonic germ cells.
source: Thus, in the absence of direct or indirect continuous exposure, Δ9-THC still has lasting consequences on the metabolome of embryonic germ cells.
evidence: Supported by metabolic profiling data in PGCLCs derived from exposed precursors.

claim: Nutrient stress induces oocyte metabolites remodelling that drives the onset of metabolic diseases in the progeny in Drosophila.
source: A recent study in Drosophila reported that nutrient stress induces oocyte metabolites remodelling that drives the onset of metabolic diseases in the progeny (Hocaoglu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hocaoglu et al., 2021.

claim: Non-DNA-associated factors, such as germline metabolites, can act as factors of inheritance.
source: This indicates that non-DNA-associated factors, such as germline metabolites, can act as factors of inheritance.
evidence: Supported by inference from the Drosophila study cited.

claim: Exposure to Δ9-THC remodels ESCs and EpiLCs metabolome and a metabolic memory of this exposure is retained during PGCLCs differentiation.
source: Similarly, we show here that exposure to Δ9-THC remodels ESCs and EpiLCs metabolome and that a metabolic memory of this exposure is retained during PGCLCs differentiation (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data across developmental stages.

claim: Despite proliferation and a higher number of cells, the number of DEGs that were downregulated in PGCLCs deriving from Δ9-THC-exposed ESCs and EpiLCs suggests a general degradation of PGCLCs' homeostasis.
source: In addition to metabolic remodelling, we show that the PGCLCs transcriptome is also altered. In particular, despite proliferation and a higher number of cells, the number of DEGs that were downregulated in PGCLCs deriving from Δ9-THC-exposed ESCs and EpiLCs suggests a general degradation of PGCLCs' homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing predominantly downregulated genes.

claim: Perinatal Δ9-THC exposure has been associated with alteration in cell adhesion in the central nervous system, with an impact on neuronal interactions and morphology.
source: During the development of the central nervous system, perinatal Δ9-THC exposure has also been associated with alteration in cell adhesion, with an impact on neuronal interactions and morphology (Gómez et al., 2007; Keimpema et al., 2011; Kittler et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gómez et al., 2007; Keimpema et al., 2011; Kittler et al., 2000.

claim: Cell-cell adhesion is crucial in PGCs' formation both in cell culture systems as well as in vivo where it controls PGCs motility during their migration towards the developing somatic gonad.
source: Cell-cell adhesion is crucial in PGCs' formation both in cell culture systems (Okamura et al., 2003) as well as in vivo where it controls PGCs motility during their migration towards the developing somatic gonad (Barton et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okamura et al., 2003; Barton et al., 2016.

claim: Exposure to Δ9-THC prior to specification affects embryonic germ cells' transcriptome and metabolome, which could have adverse consequences on cell-cell adhesion with an impact on PGC normal development in vivo.
source: Our results thus show that exposure to Δ9-THC prior to specification affects embryonic germ cells' transcriptome and metabolome. This in turn could have adverse consequences on cell-cell adhesion with an impact on PGC normal development in vivo.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomics and metabolomics data, with speculation about in vivo consequences.

claim: In vitro models for germ cell development offer a unique opportunity for studies on the molecular mechanisms involved in the inheritance of exposure.
source: In vitro models for germ cell development offer a unique opportunity for such studies (Verdikt et al., 2022) and our work in mouse PGCLCs identifies metabolites as relevant carriers of information across developmental stages.
evidence: Supported by citation to Verdikt et al., 2022 and the experimental approach used.

claim: This work in mouse PGCLCs identifies metabolites as relevant carriers of information across developmental stages.
source: In vitro models for germ cell development offer a unique opportunity for such studies (Verdikt et al., 2022) and our work in mouse PGCLCs identifies metabolites as relevant carriers of information across developmental stages.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data showing metabolic memory across developmental stages.

claim: In vitro gametogenesis, up to the reconstitution of fully functional spermatozoa and oocytes, is a reality in mouse.
source: While in vitro gametogenesis, up to the reconstitution of fully functional spermatozoa and oocytes, is a reality in mouse (Hikabe et al., 2016; Komeya et al., 2018; Luo and Yu, 2021; Yamashiro et al., 2018), transposition to humans has been hindered by ethical and technical considerations (Luo and Yu, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hikabe et al., 2016; Komeya et al., 2018; Luo and Yu, 2021; Yamashiro et al., 2018.

claim: Transposition of in vitro gametogenesis to humans has been hindered by ethical and technical considerations.
source: While in vitro gametogenesis, up to the reconstitution of fully functional spermatozoa and oocytes, is a reality in mouse (Hikabe et al., 2016; Komeya et al., 2018; Luo and Yu, 2021; Yamashiro et al., 2018), transposition to humans has been hindered by ethical and technical considerations (Luo and Yu, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo and Yu, 2021.

claim: Protocols for human PGCLCs have been developed but proper induction to viable, fertile offspring cannot be verified.
source: For instance, protocols for human PGCLCs have been developed (Gell et al., 2020) but proper induction to viable, fertile offspring cannot be verified (Luo and Yu, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gell et al., 2020; Luo and Yu, 2021.

claim: Preliminary results in hESCs show that Δ9-THC exposure negatively impacts their global energy metabolism.
source: Nevertheless, our preliminary results in hESCs show that Δ9-THC exposure negatively impacts their global energy metabolism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Future studies will need to confirm whether metabolic reprogramming by Δ9-THC is also carried over developmental stages in human models for the germline.
source: Future studies will need to confirm whether such metabolic reprogramming is also carried over developmental stages in human models for the germline.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: This work highlights the importance of the metabolic remodelling induced by Δ9-THC and its potential role as a driver of exposure memory through differentiation stages.
source: Together, our studies reveal a moderate but significant impact of Δ9-THC exposure on early embryonic processes. Our work also highlights the importance of the metabolic remodelling induced by Δ9-THC and its potential role as a driver of exposure memory through differentiation stages.
evidence: Supported by integration of all experimental data showing metabolic memory.
